templates.pattern: A compound contains [N] atoms of element X (RAM = [RAM]) in one formula unit. The relative molecular mass of the compound is [RMM]. Calculate the percentage by mass of element X in the compound.
templates.explanation:
Percentage by mass = (n × RAM_element ÷ RMM_compound) × 100
= ([N] × [RAM] ÷ [RMM]) × 100
= [N*RAM*100] ÷ [RMM]
= [RESULT]%

This is used to find the composition of a compound and to calculate empirical formulas from experimental data.

templates.pattern: An element has two isotopes of masses [M1] and [M2]. Isotope 1 has an abundance of [AB1]%. Calculate the relative atomic mass of the element.
templates.explanation:
RAM = (M₁ × AB₁ + M₂ × AB₂) ÷ 100
= ([M1] × [AB1] + [M2] × [AB2]) ÷ 100
= ([M1*AB1] + [M2*AB2]) ÷ 100
= [RESULT]

The RAM is a weighted average — isotopes with higher abundance contribute more to the average.

templates.pattern: Calculate the relative molecular mass of a molecule containing [C] carbon atoms (RAM=12), [H] hydrogen atoms (RAM=1) and [O] oxygen atoms (RAM=16).
templates.explanation:
RMM = (C × 12) + (H × 1) + (O × 16)
= ([C] × 12) + ([H] × 1) + ([O] × 16)
= [C*12] + [H] + [O*16]
= [RESULT]

The RMM is the sum of all atomic masses in the formula. It equals the mass in grams of one mole of the compound.

templates.pattern: A sample contains [MOLECULES] × 10²³ molecules of a compound. Calculate the number of moles of the compound. (Avogadro's number = 6.02 × 10²³)
templates.explanation:
Moles = number of molecules ÷ Avogadro's number
= [MOLECULES] × 10²³ ÷ 6.02 × 10²³
= [MOLECULES] ÷ 6.02
= [RESULT] mol

Avogadro's number applies to any type of particle — atoms, molecules, ions or formula units.

templates.pattern: The [N]th electron shell of an atom can hold a maximum of how many electrons? Use the formula 2n².
templates.explanation:
Maximum electrons = 2n²
= 2 × [N]²
= 2 × [N*N]
= [RESULT]

Shell 1: 2, Shell 2: 8, Shell 3: 18, Shell 4: 32, Shell 5: 50. Higher shells have sub-shells (s, p, d, f) which divide up this capacity.

templates.pattern: An atom of atomic number [Z] loses [L] electrons to form a cation. How many electrons does the cation contain?
templates.explanation:
Electrons in cation = atomic number − electrons lost
= [Z] − [L]
= [RESULT]

The proton number stays the same when ions form. Only the electron count changes. A cation has fewer electrons than protons giving it a positive charge.

templates.pattern: An atom has atomic number [Z] and a shielding constant of [S]. Calculate the effective nuclear charge experienced by the outermost electrons.
templates.explanation:
Effective nuclear charge Z_eff = Z − σ
= [Z] − [S]
= [RESULT]

Inner electrons partially shield outer electrons from the full nuclear attraction. Effective nuclear charge increases across a period — this explains why atomic radius decreases across a period.

templates.pattern: The first ionisation energy of an element is [IE1] kJ/mol and the second ionisation energy is [IE2] kJ/mol. Calculate the ratio IE2 ÷ IE1.
templates.explanation:
Ratio = IE₂ ÷ IE₁
= [IE2] ÷ [IE1]
= [RESULT]

A very large ratio indicates the second electron is being removed from an inner shell — this element is in Group 1. Smaller ratios suggest both electrons are in the same outer shell.

templates.pattern: Atom A has atomic number [Z1] and atomic radius [R1] pm. Atom B has atomic number [Z2] and is in the same period. Estimate the atomic radius of atom B in pm using the Zeff relationship.
templates.explanation:
Atomic radius ∝ 1 ÷ Z_eff
R₂ ≈ R₁ × Z₁ ÷ Z₂
= [R1] × [Z1] ÷ [Z2]
= [RESULT] pm

Atomic radius decreases across a period because increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer without adding new shells.

templates.pattern: A sample contains [ATOMS] × 10²³ atoms of element X (RAM = [RAM]). Calculate the mass of the sample in grams. (Avogadro's number = 6.02 × 10²³)
templates.explanation:
Moles = [ATOMS] × 10²³ ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ = [ATOMS] ÷ 6.02
Mass = moles × RAM
= ([ATOMS] ÷ 6.02) × [RAM]
= [RESULT] g

This two-step calculation connects the number of atoms to a measurable mass — essential in experimental chemistry.
